title: Bumpless pipe dreams encode Gr"obner geometry of Schubert polynomials: the ASM ideal facts (Lemma 2.6)
author: Patricia Klein and Anna Weigandt
work: Bumpless pipe dreams encode Gr"obner geometry of Schubert polynomials
difficulty_reason: The counted lemma is the technical heart of the article’s first half: it is the statement that the ASM ideal of an alternating sign matrix is the intersection of the initial ideals indexed by its essential permutations, that it is radical, that its irredundant prime decomposition is the intersection of the matrix Schubert ideals I_u over u in Perm(A), that its height is the height of A, and that equidimensionality of the matrix and of Spec(R/I_A) agree. Its proof is not a citation and not a formal consequence of the definition of an ASM ideal. Even with the Knutson-Miller theorem (the context Theorem 2.4), the Fulton prime/height/Cohen-Macaulay facts (the context Proposition 2.3), Weigandt’s Proposition 4.8 on the Stanley-Reisner complexes of pipe dreams, the Lascoux-Schutzenberger and Reiner decompositions of an ASM as a join of bigrassmannian permutations and Miller-Sturmfels Lemma 15.19 on incomparable Schubert ideals supplied as named prerequisites, the authors must still construct the two-sided chain of containments eq:idealcontainments, recognise the two outer ideals as squarefree monomial ideals whose Stanley-Reisner complexes are respectively the intersection and the union of the pipe-dream complexes, invoke Weigandt’s identity to collapse that chain into equalities, transfer the resulting equality of initial ideals to an equality of the ideals themselves by comparing Hilbert functions, and then run the bigrassmannian reduction twice to reach radicality and the irredundant prime decomposition. Assembling those five imported tools into a single working argument - and knowing which of them applies at which of the six parts - is research-level commutative algebra and combinatorics rather than a qualification exercise, although every individual ingredient is a quoted theorem, which is what places the unit in the middle of the scale rather than at its top.
